title: TA9-16084
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of El Salvador, seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 The claimant's identity has been established through a certified copy of her passport.2 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant fears returning to El Salvador because she alleges that she was a victim of attempted extortion by the MS-18 (Maras) The claimant made the following allegations in the narrative of her Personal Information Form (PIF):3
The claimant was an XXXX XXXX for a XXXXcompany and owned a small XXXX XXXX XXXX. Between the two businesses, she derived an average monthly income of US$800.

Between XXXX XXXX, 2006 and XXXX XXXX, 2006, the claimant was threatened and required to pay money on an ongoing basis to members of the Maras. On one occasion, the claimant was beaten and had clothing stolen from her business.
On XXXX XXXX, 2006, the claimant was mugged by two men and robbed of her money and jewels.
The claimant travelled to the United States of America (US) on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2009 and made a claim for refugee protection on the same date.

I find that the risk faced by the claimant is a generalized rather than a personalized risk, which falls under the paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA exception because protection is limited to those who face a specific risk that is not generally faced by others in or from that country. I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.
The determinative issues in this claim are nexus and generalized risk. Nexus

I have considered whether the claimant has a nexus to one of the five Convention refugee grounds, namely, race, religion, nationality, real or imputed political opinion or membership in a particular social group.

The claimant testified that she fears members of the Maras, who were attempting to extort money from her and threatening her life. The claimant testified that she had two incomes; one from her employment at a XXXX company and one from a XXXX XXXX she owned and operated out of her home. The claimant testified that she earned approximately US$800 monthly which was more than five times the average salary earned in El Salvador, as the average income at that time was roughly US$150. The claimant testified she believes that the Maras targeted her because they were aware of her business and that she derived a monthly income, and as such, they knew they could get money from her.

The claimant testified that between XXXX 2006 and XXXX 2006, she had been approached and threatened for money on a number of occasions. She testified that during each of these encounters, nothing other than money had ever been demanded of her.

Counsel submitted that to consider the issue of nexus, the risk and circumstances must be considered from the perspective of the agent of persecution, namely the Maras. Counsel submitted that the El Salvadorian government experiences great difficulty in dealing with the Maras and as the Maras' motive for extortion is to further their cause and not for reasons of simple criminality, it would constitute an imputed political opinion.

The members of the Maras were demanding money and they knew where the claimant's business was located. This leads me to conclude that the objective behind this extortion was purely criminal in nature, rather than being targeted as a consequence of real or imputed political opinion, as counsel argues. The robbery, assault and threats against the claimant were purely consequential when she refused to accede to the extortion demands of the Maras.

The country documentary evidence4 states that the Maras engage in economically motivated crimes involving extortion and kidnapping for ransom. Having reviewed the evidence in its entirety, including the circumstances particular to this claimant, I find that the claimant was targeted by the Maras for the purpose of extortion, as is the modus operandi of the Maras in El Salvador. Insufficient reliable and probative evidence was adduced in the particulars of this case to indicate that the motive of the Maras was anything other than criminal in nature, to extort money from someone they perceived to have an ability to pay. I find that in making demands for money, the Maras were acting in a criminal manner, which does not provide the claimant with a link to one of the Convention refugee grounds.

I find the claimant is a victim of crime and was not sought out by the Maras for any reason, other than the fact that she had a perceived wealth based on her being a business owner. 'Perceived wealth' does not constitute membership in a particular social group.

The Federal Court has held that victims of crime, corruption,5 or vendettas6 generally fail to establish a link between their fear of persecution, and one of the Convention grounds in the definition of Convention refugee. The Board has been upheld in its finding of lack of nexus, where the claimant was a target of a personal vendetta,7 or where the claimant was a victim of crime.8

I conclude that the claimant is a target as a victim of crime or vendetta, which does not provide the claimant with a nexus to a Convention refugee ground. Therefore, the claimant is not a Convention refugee, and the claim under section 96 of the IRPA fails. The balance of the analysis in this decision is pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA. Generalized Risk

The harm feared by the claimant does not amount to a personalized risk to her life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. The courts have expressed the view that consideration of an application under section 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA requires a personalized review in the context of the actual and potential risks to which the claimant is subject. In cases like this, where the general public is subject to the risk of crime, the fact that some individuals are more exposed to the risk, because they live in more dangerous areas or because they are perceived as being wealthier, does not necessarily make her a person in need of protection. A person who is a direct victim of crime is not a person in need of protection within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.9 Documentary evidence indicates that crime is prevalent in El Salvador. The Overseas Security Advisory Counsel states that El Salvador is "one of the most violent countries in the world," and that extortion is one of the methods used to finance the criminal groups.10

The claimant testified that she feared returning to El Salvador because she believes she would be killed by the Maras for not having obeyed their extortion demands. The claimant testified that she had been contacted numerous times beginning in XXXX 2006 by members of the Maras who were demanding money. The claimant testified that she had also been a victim of robbery and had been thrown against a wall and beaten, for not complying with the monetary demands of the Maras. The claimant testified that she believed she was personally targeted because the members of the Maras thought she had an ability to meet their demands because they were aware that she owned her own business. The claimant was asked if she was aware of others who had been similarly threatened for money by members of the Maras; she testified that she was, and that she knew through the news that people who owned businesses, who had refused to give the Maras the money they demanded, were murdered.

Based on the totality of the evidence, I find that the claimant was a victim of extortion which is a generalized risk faced by others who are perceived to be successful business people in El Salvador.

Even though the claimant may have been specifically targeted by the Maras, everyone in El Salvador faces a similar risk as the claimant experienced. It is not just the fear of the risk, which is a section 96 of the IRPA analysis. To succeed under section 97 of the IRPA, the risk must be a personal or individualized risk and must be likely to occur on a balance of probabilities, and that risk "would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country." Too many decision-makers - judges and RPD members - have made the error of saying or implying that a generalized risk is by definition not a personalized risk. In fact, if a claimant faces no personal risk, there would be no point in analyzing whether his or her claim fell under the generalized risk exception. It is required by s. 97 that the risk faced by the claimant the personal. Too many decision-makers inaccurately describe, or fail entirely to describe, the risk faced by the claimants. Before determining whether the risk faced by a claimant is one generally faced by others, the decision-makers must (a) make an expressed determination of what the risk is; (b) determine whether that risk is a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment; and (c) clearly express and the basis for the risk.11

In this case, it is accepted that the claimant was subjected personally to a risk of harm under section 97 of the Act. Members of the Maras targeted the claimant due to the perception of wealth, based on her being a business owner. In accordance with the documentary evidence, the risk faced by the claimant as a result of being a target of extortion is faced generally by all people in El Salvador who are perceived to have the means to pay the demanded money. The extortion would be faced in every part of the country and is faced generally by all individuals in El Salvador. The evidence in this case shows that the fear of extortion has been recognized as a generalized risk. A generalized risk does not have to affect everyone in the same way. The Federal Court has upheld the Board in finding generalized risk for various victims of Maras Salvatrucha.12

Extortion is part of Maras Salvatrucha's modus operandi and constitutes a widespread risk for all citizens of El Salvador. The MS-13 strikes terror in the entire El Salvadorian population. The claimant was one of their many such victims. The fact that the claimant had been identified personally as a target does not necessarily remove her from the generalized risk category, since the nature of the risk is one that is faced generally by others in the country.

I have reviewed the jurisprudence relating to generalized risk, and in this connection, I considered the case of Vickram,13 a businessman of Indo-Guyanese origin, who was threatened, beaten and harassed repeatedly by a group of black bandits in Guyana, and was determined to have been victimized due to his profile of belonging to a wealthy business family. The Federal Court upheld the Board's determination that the risk faced by that claimant14 was criminal activity and was no greater than that faced by the population at large, and that the perception of wealth does not constitute a particularized risk under section 97 of the Act.

While their case differs from the present case, I am of the view that if the risk of violence, injury or crime is a generalized risk faced by all citizens of El Salvador, the fact that a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently, does not mean that they are not subject to a "generalized risk" of violence. The fact that they share the same risk as other persons similarly situated does not make their risk a "personalized risk" subject to protection under section 97 of the Act.

Counsel submitted Martinez Pineda,15 however, that case is not consistent with the predominant line of cases such as Acosta, Perez, and Guifarro.16 In any event, Martinez Pineda and a case similar to it, Zacarias,17 the Court ruled that the Board must consider the specific circumstances of the claimants, which I have done. Referring to the other cases I have mentioned, Acosta was facing death at the hands of the Maras for inadvertently failing to pay the extortion money taken from bus drivers and fare collectors. Guifarro faced retaliation for not complying with the extortion demands of the Maras and reporting them to the police. That, however, did not turn their risk as one of many such victims of these gangs into a personalized risk. In Acosta, the Court stated that victims of generalized violence are often known to the perpetrators, by name, by position, or for any number of different reasons. The fact that the victims of generalized violence have an identity, as all people do, and that that identity is or becomes known to the perpetrator, does not mean that they are not a victim of generalized violence. Furthermore, regarding generalized risk in Guifarro:18 The Court underscored that it is now settled law that claims will not meet the requirements of section 97(1)(b(ii) of the IRPA where (i) targeting is because of the claimant's membership in a sub-group of persons returning from abroad or perceived to have wealth for other reasons and (ii) that sub-group is sufficiently large that the risk can reasonably be characterized as being widespread or prevalent in that country. A sub-group numbering in the thousands would be sufficiently large as to render the risk widespread or prevalent and therefore "general" even though that sub-group may only constitute a small percentage of the general population in that country.

Furthermore, consequential harm experienced by persons who are targeted by criminal elements does not necessarily mean that their risk is personalized/not generalized, whether risk of actual or threatened violence is faced generally by others and not specific to the claimant. In summary, the fact, * that a person or group of people may be victimized repeatedly or more frequently by criminals, for example, because of their perceived wealth or because they live any more dangerous area, * that the claimant continues to be pursued after reporting to police or relocating, * that the claimant faces retaliation for not complying with the demands of the criminals, does not remove the risk from the exception, if it is one faced generally by others. The consequential harm faced in the circumstances does not mean that the risk is not a generalized one.19

As stated in Ventura De Parada,20 this claimant was not targeted personally; rather, she, as a business person, who was perceived to be well-off, had been targeted. That was not a personalized risk and the court upheld that finding. Similarly in Perez,21 the Court found that the risk faced was a generalized one.

Similarly in Prophete,22 the Federal Court helped to distinguish what constitutes generalized risk. The case was similar on the facts, to the one before the panel. Mr. Prophete was a citizen of Haiti who sought asylum in Canada. He was a victim of violence in Haiti because he was a successful businessman there and he was perceived to be wealthy. The Federal Court found that: ...the applicant does not face a personalized risk that is not faced by other individuals in or from Haiti. The risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haitians. While a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their wealth, all Haitians are at risk of becoming victims of violence.23
In other words, in a country such as El Salvador, much like Haiti, plagued with violence, criminality destabilizes the country and all citizens are subjected to that risk.

Counsel also submitted that similar to Gomez24 the risk to this claimant is personalized as a result of the claimant defying the demands of the gang, making the threats and assaults more than general I nature. I do not find that this occurred in the particular case at hand. Insufficient reliable and probative evidence was forwarded to indicate that the risk to this particular claimant had changed, or was different from that which others in El Salvador face as a result of non-compliance to the extortion demands of the Maras.

I find the claimant was a victim of crime. The threats to the claimant occurred as a result of extortion demands. The subsequent robbery and assault flowed as a consequence of the initial demands. Unfortunately, this behaviour on the part of the Maras is a part of their modus operandi. In accordance with the documentary evidence, the risk faced by the claimant as a result of being the target of extortion, is faced generally by many people who are perceived to be wealthy, or own their own business in El Salvador. The Federal Court has upheld the Board in finding generalized risk for various victims of Mara Salvatrucha.25

The documentary evidence suggests that the Mara gang has perpetuated much of the violence and criminality in and around the country. Extortion and robbery is a part of the Mara Salvatrucha's modus operandi, and constitutes a widespread risk for all citizens of El Salvador. The gangs strike terror in the entire El Salvadorian population. The claimant was among their many such victims.

In light of the foregoing, I conclude that the risk the claimant faces would be exempted pursuant to section 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA, as her fears of the Maras is a risk faced generally by others in El Salvador.

Based on the particular facts of this case, I find that the risk faced by the claimant is a generalized rather than a personalized risk, which falls under the paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA exception of the IRPA.
Therefore, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor is she a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

Accordingly, the Refugee Protection Division rejects her claim for Refugee Protection.
